summary:
Visitors in Normandie stand under France's national framework. The rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law and marriage apply uniformly across all regions and departments, and the sources reviewed contain no Normandie-specific transgender findings. The national inspection and oversight bodies documented below operate in the region unchanged.

The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no dedicated statutory rule. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose identity documents record a male sex, the vast majority of those held without sex-reassignment surgery, are placed in men's facilities.

A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 reports one detainee recalling inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison, illustrated in the feature by the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions Hazan describes as worrying.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records the persistence of serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees in adult prisons, while noting that none were identified in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station; Caen prison lies within Normandie and is the only establishment visited that falls in the region.

The CGLPL told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention. The 2021 opinion finds placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches still in force, records no marked improvement since 2010 despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issues binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, on the argument that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The CGLPL's 2021 opinion draws a sharp line between settings: serious violations persisted in adult prisons, whereas none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. A trans visitor held in one category of institution can therefore face materially different conditions from a resident held in another.

The 2016 legal gender-recognition reform changed how detainees are documented but did not change how they are placed. The CGLPL records no marked improvement between its 2010 opinion and its 2021 opinion, which is why the later opinion was issued at all.

The 64% identity-discrimination figure reported by the EU Fundamental Rights Agency for 2023 gives a scale to the everyday layer of risk that France's own bodies describe as persistent rather than prohibited. It concerns residents and visitors alike in services, employment and accommodation.

National figures and named establishments outside Normandie, including the Tarbes prison holding Louna and the Toulouse sites inspected by the CGLPL, are cited here as evidence of the framework that also binds establishments in the region, not as findings about Normandie itself.
localsOnly:
Residents held in French prisons are placed under Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which separates men and women into different establishments. Trans prisoners whose documents record a male sex are consequently held in men's facilities, with placement decided facility by facility rather than by statute.

Adeline Hazan's office, the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, treats transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in custody, and the CGLPL accepts letters directly from detained trans people; correspondence of that kind formed the evidentiary base of the 2021 opinion.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 is binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty, and it addresses placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches, together with the isolation of vulnerable detainees and suicide prevention.

The Défenseur des droits handles complaints of discrimination on the basis of gender identity and has issued a framework decision with guidance addressed to service providers, drawing on case files and association testimony.

Same-sex marriage has been available since the equality law of 2013, providing the recognition baseline for partners of residents and visitors alike.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Normandie-specific enforcement or inspection finding appears in the sources reviewed; the Caen prison visit is the only regional data point recorded, and it is reported as one of several sites in a national review rather than as a finding about that establishment.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented at Caen prison, or at any other establishment in the region, is not sourced.

The airport account of identity-document friction dates from March 2017, and the sources do not confirm current practice at Normandie's airports or ports.

No data on hate-crime reporting, prosecution or police treatment of trans people in the region was found in the sources reviewed.

The outcome of oral question no. 219 on Louna's placement, and any subsequent decision on her facility, is not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors in the region, and any waiting times or documentation requirements attached to it, is not addressed by the sources reviewed.
